articles.title: Revenue minister Ponguleti’s Paigah land registration plan hits CMO roadblock
articles.summary: Telangana CMO blocks proposal to allow conditional registrations of disputed Paigah lands (CS 14/CS 7), keeping them on 22-A prohibited list despite revenue push.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: A proposal by revenue minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy to allow registrations in disputed Paigah lands has run into resistance from the chief minister’s office (CMO).The disagreement centres on Paigah lands covered under civic suits (CS) 14 and CS 7 of 1958, spread across nearly 1,500 acres, mostly in the erstwhile Greater Hyderabad region. Hundreds of residential colonies, gated communities and high-rise apartment complexes have come up on these lands over the years, particularly in prime western suburbs such as Hafeezpet, Madhapur, Miyapur and surrounding areas, even as the legal battle between the state and private parties has continued for nearly six decades.A couple of weeks ago, Srinivas Reddy announced that the govt was considering permitting registrations in Paigah lands through conditional registrations. Under the proposal, registration documents would clearly state that the transactions would remain subject to the outcome of pending cases before the Supreme Court and high court.Officials point out that the state has lost several cases relating to these lands, including in the Supreme Court. Even if registrations were allowed, the lands would continue to remain on the 22-A prohibited properties list.However, despite the minister’s announcement, revenue principal secretary DS Lokesh Kumar has not issued any instructions to district collectors or the registration department. Sources said some collectors sought clarification from the govt on whether registrations could be permitted.Subsequently, the revenue department reportedly informed officials that no final decision had been taken, and that cases should be examined individually. The CMO is reportedly of the view that allowing registrations could be perceived as the govt conceding defeat in the long-running legal dispute.“The revenue department is of the opinion that GHMC had permitted the buildings including some high-rises with court orders and some registrations had taken place with the court orders. Now, there is no point in stopping them for further registrations,” a senior revenue official said.For instance Mahindra Ashvita Cooperative Housing Society in survey No. 78/2 of Hafeezpet has around 664 flats. Residents say the project obtained building permission in 2015, received an occupancy certificate from GHMC in 2018 and has been occupied ever since. They also point out that property taxes have been paid regularly over the years.“The state govt put our land and apartments in 22-A claiming it as CS 14 land and stopped registrations from Nov 2025. As the building is in 22-A, we are unable to sell our flats for children’s education, weddings and even obtain loans on the flats,” an office-bearer of the Mahindra Ashvita society told TOI.He said the residents’ association has submitted nearly 90 representations to various authorities over the past few months, but the issue remains unresolved.In Hafeezpet there are about 700 acres Paigah lands in survey no 77 to 80 of Hafeezpet, where there is a dispute between the state govt and private parties, around 430 acres of 484 acres in survey no 80 in Hafeezpet are covered by the buildings including gated communities and apartments. In survey nos 77 to 80, of Hafeezpet village decrees confirmed up to Supreme Court, but they are still under prohibition. In survey no 80, there are 484 acres of that only 50 acres are vacant, and the constructions have come up in the remaining land and residential colonies have come up.Similarly in survey no 172 of Hydernagar village near Kukatpally, of the 192 acres, the SC in June 2023, except 54 acres (under OSA No 55 of 2004), asked the private parties to establish the ownership afresh. articles.title: Several students accuse JNU professor of sexual harassment
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: At least 10 students of Jawaharlal Nehru University have accused a professor of sexual harassment, TOI has learned. The university's intern.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: At least 10 students of Jawaharlal Nehru University have accused a professor of sexual harassment, TOI has learned. The university's internal complaints committee is investigating the matter, sources said. The complaints were submitted around a month ago, according to officials aware of the proceedings.It is alleged that the professor, who lives on campus, invited students to his house for gatherings and made sexual advances, sources said. Some complaints also allege that he made lewd or inappropriate remarks during classes, sources said.Senior students came forward with similar allegations after a more recent complaint was made against the professor, according to officials.Not aware of any complaints: ProfICC declined to comment on the complaints, saying the matter was internal and was under investigation. JNU VC Santishree Dhulipudi Pandit told TOI that allegations of sexual harassment are dealt with by ICC and VC is not a member of the body.Asked if he had appeared before ICC or recorded a statement, the professor in question said he was not aware of any complaints, and that the allegations against him were false.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 2 coaches of Mahananda Express derail near Ara Railway Station
articles.summary: PATNA: Two coaches of the Alipurduar-New Delhi Mahananda Express ( 15483) derailed near Ara railway station under Danapur division of the East Central.
articles.body: PATNA: Two coaches of the Alipurduar-New Delhi Mahananda Express ( 15483) derailed near Ara railway station under Danapur division of the East Central Railway (ECR) in the early hours of Sunday. No passenger was injured in the incident.According to preliminary investigation, the incident occurred around 4 am when the loco pilot allegedly overshot a signal.After realising that the signal was not meant for his train, the loco pilot moved the train backwards towards the loop line following which two wheels of the coaches got derailed, ECR CPRO Saraswati Chandra said .Railway officials immediately rushed a rescue and restoration team to the spot.The affected track was cleared on priority and normal movement was restored after the coaches were attended to.The Mahananda Express resumed its onward journey at around 7.23am after completion of the necessary procedures, he said.Railway authorities have initiated a detailed inquiry to ascertain the exact circumstances leading to the derailment.Senior officials of the Danapur division are monitoring the situation and further action will be taken based on the findings of the investigation, sources said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: In 2013, a UK beach began planting discarded Christmas trees to trap blowing sand; by 2026, the project had created 90 metres of new dunes that help defend homes from flooding
articles.summary: UK News: Discarded Christmas trees are being used to help protect homes and businesses along the Fylde Coast in Lancashire, UK. Since the project began in 2013.
articles.body: Discarded Christmas trees are being used to help protect homes and businesses along the Fylde Coast in Lancashire, UK. Since the project began in 2013, old Christmas trees have been placed on St Annes beach to trap wind-blown sand and help build wider sand dunes.According to Fydle Council, the annual work is part of the Fylde Sand Dunes Project, which aims to restore and conserve the coastal dunes. Fylde Council, Lancashire Wildlife Trust and Blackpool Council work together on the project, which is funded by the Environment Agency.The idea is simple. Trees are placed in front of the existing dunes, where their branches slow down the wind and trap sand. As more sand collects around the trees, the mound grows and can eventually become part of a new dune.The project has already produced a visible change. Last year, more than 2,000 Christmas trees were collected from residents and used in the planting work. According to the council, this helped create a 90-metre increase in the width of the Fylde Sand Dune system.Christmas trees build dunesSand dunes naturally develop when wind-blown sand is trapped by an obstruction on the beach. At first, the collected sand can be unstable and may collapse. Plants can then begin growing in small pockets of sand and help hold the material in place.At St Annes, discarded Christmas trees act as the first obstruction. Their branches catch sand carried inland by the wind. Over time, more sand becomes trapped around the trees, allowing the dune to grow.The process then continues naturally. Pioneer grasses such as sand couch and lyme grass can grow in the dunes. Marram grass can later become more dominant as sand builds around it. Its growth helps stabilise the new dune, allowing more plants to establish.As the plants grow and spread, they help hold more sand in place. Eventually, organic matter from plants that die and decay builds up. The dune becomes more stable and develops into a habitat with different plants and animals.Why dunes matterDunes act as a natural, or ‘soft’, sea defence. During storms, they absorb some of the energy from the sea. Wider dunes are more effective at providing this protection. The dunes help reduce the risk of erosion caused by storm surges, which happen when strong winds combine with high tides.However, the dunes along the Fylde Coast are much smaller than they once were. According to the Fylde Council, more than 80% of the dunes have been lost over the past 150 years because of coastal development.The remaining dunes are now squeezed between the sea and nearby towns. This makes protecting and extending them important for both coastal communities and wildlife.Amy Pennington, Lancashire Wildlife Trust’s Fylde Sand Dunes Project Senior Engagement Officer, said the dunes provide habitat for a wide range of plants and animals and also act as a soft sea defence.“The sand dunes along the Fylde Coast are home to a diverse and specialised ecosystem, hosting a variety of unique plants and animals,” she said.A habitat for plants and wildlifeThe dunes have been designated as a Biological Heritage Site and are also a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). They support specialised plants and animals that are adapted to the dry and shifting conditions of a sand dune environment.Species found in the dunes include dune helleborine orchids, Isle of Man cabbage, dune pansies, sea holly and round-leaved wintergreen. Wildlife includes the grayling butterfly, mining bees, common lizards, skylarks, linnets and reed buntings.The environment changes as the dunes develop. Areas closer to the beach can have alkaline conditions because the sand contains pieces of sea shells. Further inland, the ground can become more acidic as the dune matures, allowing different plants to grow.As part of the project, volunteers also remove invasive plants, plant dune grasses and install paling fences to trap wind-blown sand. In addition, wetland ‘slacks’ are being created behind some dunes to support more plants and wildlife.According to Councillor Tommy Threlfall, Fylde Council’s Lead Member for Environment, the project had continued for more than a decade.“Every Christmas tree donated by our residents becomes part of something truly special,” he said. “We’re not just recycling trees, we’re building natural defences that will protect our coastal communities for generations to come,” he added.The project continues to rely on volunteers and local support. In February 2026, volunteers from across Lancashire were due to gather at St Annes beach to plant more than 2,000 donated Christmas trees.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Four private Michigan islands spanning 520 acres hit the market for $2.3 million; the deal includes a home, two boats and land protected by a conservation easement
articles.summary: US News: A private group of four islands covering 520 acres along the US-Canada border has been listed for $2.3 million. The sale includes a renovated home, ma.
articles.body: A private group of four islands covering 520 acres along the US-Canada border has been listed for $2.3 million. The sale includes a renovated home, machinery, two boats and a mainland dock slip. Located in Potagannissing Bay and the St Marys River near Drummond Island, the property includes Burnt Island, Wilson Island, Claw Island and Harris Island, according to the New York Post and listing brokers Coldwell Banker Schmidt Realtors and @properties. Burnt Island makes up most of the property and contains the main home and other facilities. Wilson, Claw and Harris Islands form a smaller group nearby. The large estate combines private wilderness with permanent conservation protections and offers about 2,000 feet of waterfront along northern Michigan’s international water boundary.Turnkey residence with panoramic water viewsThe main home sits on the southern tip of Burnt Island and offers 270-degree views of the surrounding waterways and shipping lanes. Originally built as an island retreat, the 2,131-square-foot house was fully renovated inside and outside between 2017 and 2018. The home has three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. It is being sold turnkey, with furnishings and working equipment included in the sale. "If you have ever dreamed of owning your own island, here's your chance to own four!" the listing from Gaslight Group Properties and Coldwell Banker says. "Set along the picturesque northern border in the St Mary's River & Potagannissing Bay, this group of islands is truly special." The sale also includes a utility truck, a Kubota tractor with a brush hog attachment, a riding lawn mower, a separate sauna building and two motorboats to help with maintenance and travel between the islands. The property’s two main docks and protective breakwalls were rebuilt between 2022 and 2023. The sale also comes with a dedicated boat slip at DeTour Village on the Michigan mainland, providing regular access to the islands.Environmental protection and native wildlife corridorsOne of the main features of the 520-acre property is the balance between private use and long-term environmental protection. About 420 acres across the four islands are covered by a permanent conservation easement held by the Little Traverse Conservancy, a regional land trust in northern Michigan. The easement prevents future commercial subdivision and major construction, helping protect native forests and wildlife habitats. The owner still has about 100 acres of unrestricted land around the home, outbuildings and shorelines for private recreation and personal use. "Most of the 520 acres is protected by a conservation easement with Little Traverse Conservancy but about 100 of the acres and the shorelines are yours to explore," according to the official Northern Michigan MLS listing. The islands feature private walking trails, wild fruit orchards with apple and crabapple trees, milkweed meadows and quiet coves. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters, beavers, coyotes and white-tailed deer. The waters around Potagannissing Bay are also an established fishing area, supporting native populations of walleye, smallmouth bass, yellow perch and cisco.Remote border real estate market dynamicsThe property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. People staying on Burnt Island can often watch commercial Great Lakes freighters travelling through the nearby St Marys River channel, which connects Lake Superior with Lake Huron. Real estate agents who specialise in northern Michigan waterfront properties say turnkey island estates with mainland facilities, such as dedicated marina slips, can command higher prices because of the challenges of maintaining remote properties. Listing agents Sam DeCamp and Anna DeCamp of Gaslight Group Properties are continuing to show the property to potential buyers looking for private conservation retreats.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India backs UN world map resolution but calls out inaccurate J&K depiction
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Sunday said India had voted in favour of a United Nations General Assembly resolution promoting the use.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Sunday said India had voted in favour of a United Nations General Assembly resolution promoting the use of equal-area world map projections. It also made it clear that the measure does not endorse any particular map and that India’s sovereign territory must be depicted according to its official map.The MEA said the resolution neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map and does not address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names.India nevertheless used its explanation of vote to reiterate its position on Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.“India’s sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India’s official map. Any inaccurate or misleading depiction is unacceptable. Our position on India’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear, consistent and non-negotiable.”The UN General Assembly adopted the resolution, titled “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa”, on September 4 by a vote of 164 to one.The resolution encourages the use of equal-area projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses. However, India clarified that it should not be interpreted as endorsing any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries.“We believe that the resolution should be understood as supporting the broader use and consideration of equal-area map projections and not as endorsing the Equal Earth projection or any other specific map projection,” Indian diplomat Raghoo Puri said while explaining India’s vote.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Pennsylvania couple faced a $13.4 million price tag for 182 acres; a conservation deal instead kept most of the land under permanent development restrictions
articles.summary: US News: In the mid-2000s, an undeveloped stretch of Bucks County, Pennsylvania, known as Rorer Tract, contained woodlands and cleared land used for farming. B.
articles.body: In the mid-2000s, an undeveloped stretch of Bucks County, Pennsylvania, known as Rorer Tract, contained woodlands and cleared land used for farming. But its zoning allowed the property to be developed into single-family homes, and a development scenario that was prepared for the land showed that its full commercial potential could accommodate at least 60 homes, while a clustered approach could potentially have produced as many as 218 residential units.Phyllis McGrady and Christopher Antoniacci already owned neighboring property, and held an option to purchase the Rorer Tract. Three appraisals eventually produced a required purchase price of $13.4 million. The couple could not afford that amount and terminated the option in July 2006. The decision became the starting point for a complicated conservation agreement that involved the landowners, the township, the couple and Heritage Conservancy.Conservation became an alternative to full developmentIn 2005, the township and Heritage Conservancy identified the Rorer Tract and the neighboring McGrady-Antoniacci properties as among the area's most significant remaining undeveloped properties. The conservation organization became involved as the parties looked for a way to protect the land without simply leaving its development value on the table.The original development scenarios were gradually replaced by a conservation subdivision plan. The plan concentrated homes in specific areas while placing conservation easements over the surrounding land, rather than allowing the entire tract to be divided into conventional residential lots. Development was not necessarily eliminated from every acre, but the amount and location of development were sharply constrained.The development rights were worth millionsThe Rorers agreed to sell a conservation easement over their tract to Upper Makefield Township for $5.615 million, and at the same time, Heritage Conservancy agreed to purchase the 182-acre property, subject to that easement, for $6.085 million. The two transactions, together with tax considerations, brought the economics of the deal close to the $13.4 million value that had previously been established for the property.The easement was formally conveyed on June 28, 2007, and the deed transferring the property to Heritage was executed the following month. The arrangement meant that the land could change hands without returning to the development potential reflected in the earlier appraisal. The $5.615 million was payment for development rights that were being removed from the property, not simply a purchase of 182 acres.Some homes were still part of the final planThe final plan approved by Upper Makefield Township allowed Heritage to sell 10 residential lots to developer Richard Zaveta for $5.175 million, and an additional lot was sold to another buyer for $425,000. The homes were concentrated along an access road rather than scattered across the full property, and the plan also placed conservation easements over the surrounding acreage.A later description of the transaction noted that the access road for the 10 residences was designed, where possible, to follow the existing gravel farm road, and the aim was to limit disturbance to the surrounding land.A neighboring couple remained part of the dealMcGrady and Antoniacci had already owned two neighboring parcels that totaled taling 45 acres and had approached Heritage about preserving the Rorer property. As negotiations progressed, they donated land and a conservation easement of their own and contributed $275,000 in cash and common stock toward Heritage's transaction costs. They also eventually bought a 37-acre piece carved from the larger property.That parcel was already covered by conservation easements, which means it could not be developed. The couple's purchase therefore increased their overall landholding while leaving the additional acreage under permanent development restrictions. The conservation arrangement was later examined in federal tax litigation involving McGrady and Antoniacci. The Tax Court's 2016 decision addressed the couple's claimed charitable deductions and the complex series of land transfers used to assemble the final conservation plan.What was preservedCourt records describe the Rorer Tract as a mixture of woodlands and cleared agricultural land, surrounded by properties that were also subject to development pressure, but its location made the acreage significant. The zoning rules allowed the 182 acres to be developed as single-family residential property without conservation restrictions. Depending on the development model, dozens or potentially hundreds of homes could have occupied the tract. Instead, the final arrangement concentrated residential construction into a much smaller portion of the landscape and subjected the rest to conservation easements.Eleven residential lots were ultimately part of the approved development plan, while the broader tract remained protected from the kind of unrestricted subdivision that had driven its $13.4 million valuation.The transaction also shows why conservation easements can command substantial prices, and the land itself remains privately owned and can continue to change hands, but a valuable part of its potential future use is permanently restricted.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India supplied 60% of diesel to Europe in August as Russian, US supplies plunge: Report
articles.summary: India News: India supplied about 60 per cent of the diesel transiting through the Bab-el-Mandeb towards Europe in August, strengthening its role as a key source o.
articles.body: India supplied about 60 per cent of the diesel transiting through the Bab-el-Mandeb towards Europe in August, strengthening its role as a key source of refined fuel as Russian exports remain depressed and US shipments begin to decline, according to a report.Around 2,00,000 barrels per day of diesel, or gasoil, crossed the strategic shipping route for Europe last month, close to year-earlier levels after flows nearly stalled in March and April. Indian refiners accounted for roughly 60 per cent of that volume, energy analytics firm Vortexa said in a report.India, the world’s fourth-largest refiner, has 258.1 million tonnes per annum of installed capacity, above domestic fuel demand. It exported 61.5 million tonnes of petroleum products in 2025-26, making it a major global supplier, PTI reported.However, sustaining these flows could become difficult. India’s crude and condensate imports fell to about 3.8 million barrels per day in August from 4.8 million barrels per day a year earlier, data showed.Russian diesel exports averaged only around 1,50,000 barrels per day during the first 25 days of August, down about 6,10,000 barrels per day year-on-year and 81 per cent below the five-year seasonal average.The scheduled easing of Russia’s diesel export ban from September 1 may not quickly restore supplies, with Ukrainian drone strikes continuing to disrupt refineries and export infrastructure. Vortexa recorded 32 refinery attacks across July and August.The Perm refinery, with capacity of 2,60,000 barrels per day, was left operating at only about 28 per cent of its crude distillation capacity after an attack, while no diesel cargoes have left Tuapse since a May strike.The US supplied about half of Europe’s seaborne diesel imports from outside the region in August, at around 5,20,000 barrels per day. But shipments fell from nearly 5,40,000 barrels per day in the first half of August to about 3,50,000 barrels per day in the second half.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1990, cheetah expert Laurie Marker sold her possessions to begin fieldwork in Namibia; her research base now helps protect about 158,000 acres of cheetah country
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Laurie Marker sold her possessions to create the Cheetah Conservation Fund in Namibia, safeguarding 158,000 acres of cheetah habitat while fostering coexistence with local farmers.
articles.body: In 1990, American zoologist Laurie Marker made a decision that reshaped her career and eventually led to one of the world’s best-known cheetah conservation organisations. Marker founded the Cheetah Conservation Fund (CCF) that year, selling her possessions to purchase an old Land Rover for her upcoming fieldwork. She then transferred her research to Namibia, where she permanently relocated in 1991. Following her relocation, she began building a conservation programme around the survival of wild cheetahs outside conventional protected areas.In 1977, Marker first travelled to what was then South West Africa while researching whether a captive-born cheetah could learn to hunt in the wild. Marker studied Khayam’s behaviour after taking the animal from Wildlife Safari in Oregon to Namibia. This experience helped her to see another challenge that would become central to her career: wild cheetahs were being killed by livestock farmers who regarded them as threats to their animals.A conservation organisation that started from a research projectThough the CCF was established in 1990, Laurie Marker’s ultimate relocation to Namibia came in 1991. To start her field operations, she began working directly out of a local farmhouse, taking her research and conservation efforts into the farming areas where many of the country’s free-ranging cheetahs lived.As Namibia’s cheetahs often occupied private farmland, their survival was connected directly to livestock production. CCF therefore started interacting with the farmers to understand why cheetahs were being killed and to work on methods that could reduce livestock risk without resorting to lethal predator control.A peer-reviewed review of cheetah conservation programmes describes the organisation’s work in Namibia as an example of conservation outside protected areas. Moreover, it emphasises reducing conflict between cheetahs and livestock farmers.Science became the foundation of the programmeMarker’s work was not simply limited to fieldwork. During the 1980s she worked with scientists from the Smithsonian Institution and National Cancer Institute on the species’ genetic characteristics and reproductive biology. Those studies indicated unusually low genetic diversity and poor sperm quality in cheetahs, findings that helped scientists understand some of the species’ biological vulnerabilities.According to the foundation, its Namibian cheetah population study began in 1990 and used tissue and scat samples to identify individual animals and investigate population structure. The organisation has reportedly accumulated hundreds of tissue samples and more than 1,000 scat samples, creating a long-term record for ongoing and subsequent research.As cheetahs are wide-ranging predators, conserving them requires more than just protecting isolated animals. Consequently, CCF’s research included population monitoring, genetics, ecology and studies of how the species interact with farms and other lands. One such practical response to livestock conflict was suggested in 1994, when the organisation began its livestock guarding dog programme. The organisation now breeds and places Anatolian dogs and Kangal dogs with farmers, using their presence around livestock herds to deter predators and reduce attack risks. This programme demonstrates how the organisation sought to provide practical measures that could address the same concerns that had once driven much of the conflict, instead of treating farmers as an obstacle to their conservation.The small-scale operation that began with a farmhouse and an old Land Rover eventually grew into the Cheetah Conservation Fund’s International Research and Education Centre in Namibia. The place is now a multidisciplinary facility which incorporates research, veterinary work, genetics, education and model-farm activities.Today, theCheetah Conservation Fund’sInternational Research and Education Centre operates a 142,483-acre private wildlife reserve. To expand its protection footprint, the organization integrates this model facility with an additional 15,517 acres of adjacent community conservancy lands. Managed cooperatively, this joint framework fulfills the headline's scope by putting roughly 158,000 total acres of cheetah country under structural protection. The purpose of the Namibian operation was not simply to create a large fenced refuge and remove cheetahs from human-dominated landscapes. Instead, the foundation made it a point to focus on farmland, where maintaining viable predator populations depends on reducing conflict and finding ways for livestock production and wildlife to coexist.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Shameful, nasty’: Singapore minister hits out at anti-India racism after Nepal floods
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Singapore senior minister K Shanmugam has condemned racist and xenophobic online comments targeting India calling them “shameful, nasty, totally unacc.
articles.body: Singapore senior minister K Shanmugam has condemned racist and xenophobic online comments targeting India calling them “shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable”.Police are investigating the comments, which were posted online in connection with the China-Nepal disaster, Shanmugam said on Saturday.“The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” said Shanmugam, who is also Singapore’s home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security.“I have asked police to look into these comments,” he added.Shanmugam said the ministry of digital development and information would also approach social media platforms to seek the removal of comments that violate their guidelines.The comments emerged amid discussions surrounding the devastating disaster in Nepal.Shanmugam cited several examples of racist remarks posted online about the missing Singaporeans, including comments such as “no, they are not our own”. He noted that certain terms used were derogatory towards Indians.Singapore is one of India’s key economic partners and the largest trade partner in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).Meanwhile, Nepal continues to grapple with the aftermath of the disaster triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26. The resulting surge of water and debris through the Bhotekoshi River devastated settlements across northern and central Nepal.According to Nepal Police, the death toll stood at 1,344, while nearly 5,000 people remained missing. More than 13,100 people have been rescued.Authorities have faced difficulties identifying the dead, with many bodies severely damaged, decomposed or recovered in parts. Nepal Police has begun collecting DNA samples from relatives of missing people to help identify unclaimed bodies and human remains.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A California farming couple kept the development rights to their 624-acre ranch; in 2004, they took $1 million well below market to permanently block development
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Greg and Amanda Jones thwarted development on their 624-acre Redgate Ranch in California by selling a conservation easement for $1 million, ensuring its protection for future generations while maintaining ownership.
articles.body: In 2004, Greg and Amanda Jones chose to protect their property through a conservation easement, accepting far less than the land's potential development value in exchange for keeping the ranch intact. According to the Peninsula Open Space Trust, Redgate Ranch is a 624-acre property in San Gregorio, California, where Greg and Amanda Jones made a bargain sale of a conservation easement in 2004. POST paid $1 million for the easement, an amount well below market value, allowing the Joneses to retain ownership while permanently protecting the ranch from development. The agreement protected the property's scenic and natural values and ensured that the land would remain open, while the family continued to use it primarily as a working farm and weekend retreat.A ranch caught between farming and developmentRedgate Ranch is located in San Gregorio, situated along Highway 84, in California's coastal area. In the year 2000, the Jones family purchased the property, which was originally part of Souza Ranch. Instead of viewing the 624 acres as an investment in real estate, the couple operated it as a farm and used it as their getaway place. At the time the conservation plan was put into effect, approximately 150 acres were cultivated for growing red oats for hay purposes. The remainder of the ranch includes open grassland, coastal scrub, and coastal oak and mixed coniferous forest. Furthermore, there are two streams feeding into San Gregorio Creek that border the ranch property.However, the location of the ranch made it susceptible to the pressures of development. As the San Gregorio Valley became increasingly valuable for housing and other kinds of development due to its closeness to Silicon Valley and to the coast, the owners of Redgate Ranch had to face a choice that is all too common for farmers whose land borders expanding urban development zones. The choice was between retaining the land and living with the financial limitations that come with it or developing it by constructing buildings.They sold the development rights, not the ranchIn November 2004, Greg and Amanda Jones entered into a bargain sale with the Peninsula Open Space Trust (POST), offering a conservation easement over Redgate Ranch along with a pledge to donate a corridor for a future public trail. POST paid $1 million for the easement, an amount well below market value. The arrangement allowed the Joneses to retain ownership of the 624-acre ranch while permanently restricting development. The family continued to use the property as a working farm and weekend retreat, raising red oats for hay on about 150 acres and restoring grassland elsewhere to improve wildlife habitat.According to POST, without the agreement, at least four estate houses could have been built on the ranch. The additional trail easement also helped connect the property with surrounding protected lands and preserve a route for future public recreation. The arrangement demonstrates why conservation easements can be attractive to farmers and ranchers who do not want to give up their land. The owner retains the title and can continue agricultural activities, while the conservation organisation receives the legal right to enforce restrictions on future development. A study in Land Use Policy examining 157 agricultural conservation easements in the San Francisco Bay Area found that such easements can serve as a farmland-preservation and growth-management tool by permanently retiring development rights. The researchers also noted that farmland on the rural-urban fringe faces persistent pressure from development.Protection that outlasts ownershipThe significance of the ruling in 2004 is more apparent when one looks at the history of Redgate Ranch after that period. Indeed, the Joneses ended up selling the actual land. According to public records, a 624-acre Redgate Ranch was sold in January 2022 for $9.65 million. However, the conservation easement was still in place and, therefore, the sale did not undo the loss of the development rights.For the Jones family, this solution enabled them to disconnect the future of their ranch from the economic realities of the California coast real estate market. They were free to continue with their farming operations on the ranch and forfeited their right to benefit economically from the development of their land. This case demonstrates the fact that farmland is not always valued based on the market price of its sale. A ranch can serve as an agricultural area, habitat for wildlife, open land, and scenic landscape. Once the right of development is sold, this value remains intact despite any changes in ownership. Over 18 years later, the Redgate Ranch becomes an example of a unique form of land conservation. No transfer of land ownership is necessary to preserve land from development. It is possible for a farmer or rancher to keep their land and still make a permanent choice regarding future developments on their property.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Save us, save us’: Eyewitness recalls cries from rubble after building collapses near Delhi’s Satya Niketan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cries of “save us, save us!” from children trapped under the rubble could still be heard after a building collapsed near Shiv Mandir in Del.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cries of “save us, save us!” from children trapped under the rubble could still be heard after a building collapsed near Shiv Mandir in Delhi’s Satya Niketan area on Sunday afternoon, an eyewitness said.The eyewitness, who runs a shop near the site, said he and others rushed out after hearing a loud rumbling sound.“We were sitting inside the shop when we suddenly heard a sound, like the rumble of an earthquake. We rushed out immediately. There was a lot of smoke and dust, and the entire building had collapsed,” he said.The eyewitness said several people were feared trapped inside the rubble, including children. “There are at least 25-30 children.There was a boys' PG and a girls' PG nearby. Four-five people have been rescued and two-three bodies have been recovered. More are likely to be found,” he said.He said rescue teams had pulled out four children who were still breathing and that cries could still be heard from beneath the debris.“Sounds are still coming from within the rubble — children are crying out, ‘Save us, save us!’” he said.The eyewitness also said labourers working inside the building at the time of the collapse were feared buried under the rubble. “Fruit vendors are also stuck,” he added.Another eyewitness said the collapsed building was called “Hostel Daze”, a dedicated boys’ PG that had five floors. He said the building adjacent to it had also collapsed.“All the students who were inside their rooms got trapped under the rubble. We will only know the exact number of trapped students by checking the registration records,” he said.According to the first eyewitness, construction work was being carried out in the building, including work to create a basement and rental space on the ground floor.He claimed the upper structure had been reinforced while the pillars at the bottom were weak, and alleged that the renovation work may have led to the collapse. The claims could not be independently verified.The Delhi Fire Services received a call about the collapse at around 1.33pm. Rescue teams reached the site at around 1.50pm and began search operations.Several teams, including Search and Rescue, Breathing Apparatus and Water Bowser units, have been deployed at the site. Rescue operations are continuing as emergency personnel search for those trapped under the rubble.BJP MLA from RK Puram Anil Kumar Sharma, who was present at the site, said several students living in the PG were feared trapped inside the collapsed building. He said two children had been rescued and taken to hospital.The MLA said some of those trapped were also making phone calls from beneath the rubble, as multiple agencies continued efforts to rescue them.Rescue operations are still underway.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: A Cleveland bridge opened in 1933 and was being designed for a 2028 rehabilitation; new analysis found deeper floor-beam deterioration, forcing officials to close the 93-year-old bridge immediately
articles.summary: US News: A bridge in Cleveland, Ohio, that opened in 1933 has been closed until further notice after a recent analysis found more extensive deterioration than .
articles.body: A bridge in Cleveland, Ohio, that opened in 1933 has been closed until further notice after a recent analysis found more extensive deterioration than previously identified. Officials said the closure was ordered for public safety while engineers work on both short-term and long-term solutions.The Brookpark Road bridge, also known as the State Route 17 bridge and located near Cleveland Hopkins International Airport, is located between West 220th Street and NASA Parkway, Cleveland 19 news reported. It crosses Valley Parkway and the Cleveland Metroparks. The Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT) announced that the bridge would close immediately for emergency repairs, citing concerns about parts supporting its driving surface.The closure came as ODOT and its consultants were working towards a major rehabilitation project that had been planned for the coming years. Construction had been tentatively scheduled to begin in 2028, but further analysis during the design process changed the timeline.The latest decision followed an annual inspection of the ageing bridge. ODOT said the additional analysis found more extensive deterioration in the floor beams supporting the driving surface. Officials said the beams were badly deteriorated, and because of the condition of these structural components, they decided that keeping the bridge open could pose a safety concern.Study reveals damageThe Brookpark Road bridge had already been the subject of a rehabilitation study following its 2023 inspection.After that inspection, ODOT hired a consultant to carry out a study of the bridge and determine what work would be needed. Once the study was completed, the department began designing a major rehabilitation project earlier this year.At that stage, construction was tentatively planned to start in 2028. The bridge, which had been serving traffic since 1933, was therefore expected to remain in use until the rehabilitation work could begin.However, the design process involved further analysis of the structure. That analysis revealed that the deterioration of the floor beams was more extensive than previously understood.These beams support the driving surface of the bridge, making their condition an important part of the structure's safety. ODOT said the decision to shut the bridge was taken “out of an abundance of caution” and for “the safety of the public”.Brent Kovacs, ODOT District 12 public information officer, said officials had considered options such as reducing the load allowed on the bridge or reducing the number of lanes. However, ODOT decided that a complete closure was safer.“We always say if a roadway or a bridge is unsafe for the motoring public to be on, we’re going to close it in a minute, and that is really the case,” Kovacs said, as quoted by Fox 8.“We feel that this is the safest thing that we can do rather than reducing the load or reducing lanes or something temporary,” he said.What happens nextThe immediate closure has prompted ODOT to assess whether the major rehabilitation planned for 2028 can be moved forward or whether a temporary fix could safely allow traffic to return. Officials and consultants are now evaluating the available options.“Over the next week or two, we’re going to look at what our alternatives are and determine the best course of action,” Kovacs said.There is currently no timeline for when the bridge will reopen. The closure will remain in place while ODOT and its consultants determine the safest course of action.Traffic detoursWith the bridge closed, drivers using Brookpark Road have been asked to follow designated detours. For traffic travelling eastbound, the recommended route is through Clague Road to Interstate 480 east. Drivers should then take the SR 17/SR 237 exit.Westbound traffic will be diverted through Grayton Road to I-480 west, followed by Clague Road and then Brookpark Road.The detours are intended to keep traffic moving while the bridge remains closed. The closure affects the section of Brookpark Road between West 220th Street and NASA Parkway.ODOT has also asked motorists to be patient while officials work through the options. “Please just use patience,” Kovacs said. “We are working here as quickly as we can to figure out the best solution and the safest solution.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: London court clears extradition of Indian-origin pharmacist accused in Hyderabad murder case
articles.summary: UK News: A London court has ruled that Ajith Kumar Mupparapu, an Indian-origin pharmacist, can be extradited to India to face trial for allegedly poisoning his former wife's family and plotting murder, raising concerns about his treatment in custody.
articles.body: An Indian-origin pharmacist living in Britain can be extradited to Hyderabad to face trial over allegations that he poisoned his former wife’s family with arsenic and plotted to kill her father, a London court ruled on Friday, Reuters reported.Ajith Kumar Mupparapu, 46, is wanted in connection with the alleged attacks on his former wife, Sirisha Muttavarapu, and her family in Hyderabad in 2023, after the couple separated.Prosecutors allege that Mupparapu arranged for chilli powder and salt contaminated with arsenic to be sent to the family’s home. Relatives consumed food prepared with the ingredients while they were in Hyderabad for a family wedding in June 2023.Muttavarapu’s mother, Uma Maheshwari, died the following month. Prosecutors said testing showed arsenic levels in the family members’ blood and urine were more than 20 times the normal level.The allegations against Mupparapu also extend to an alleged plot targeting Muttavarapu’s father, Hanumantha Rao. Prosecutors say he organised attempts to kill Rao through a staged road accident, by trying to hire contract killers and through a plan to have him injected with a lethal dose of a muscle relaxant.Mupparapu’s lawyers challenged the extradition, arguing there was not enough evidence linking him to the arsenic found at the family’s home or establishing his involvement in the alleged attempts to kill Rao.They also argued that he could face torture if returned to India.Judge John Zani rejected the challenge, finding that the evidence presented established at least an arguable case against Mupparapu. The judge also accepted assurances from Indian authorities regarding his treatment in custody.Mupparapu can challenge the extradition decision at the High Court. His lawyer did not immediately comment on Friday’s ruling.Mupparapu has not been convicted of the allegations against him. The case will now proceed towards extradition unless an appeal changes the decision.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Can the US really make Hormuz safe? The dangerous battle against Iran’s sea mines
articles.summary: Middle East News: The US has spent four months conducting a covert and highly dangerous mine-clearance operation in the Strait of Hormuz, deploying Navy SEAL divers, ro.
articles.body: The US has spent four months conducting a covert and highly dangerous mine-clearance operation in the Strait of Hormuz, deploying Navy SEAL divers, robotic boats and specialised underwater craft to remove mines that have threatened one of the world's most important shipping routes.The operation, carried out largely at night and underwater, involved small teams of US Navy divers locating suspected Iranian mines with the help of unmanned boats and submersibles before destroying the explosives. The details of the mission were reported by the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the operation.The operation highlights the extraordinary difficulty of reopening the strategically vital waterway, where the threat of mines has compounded missile and drone attacks and sharply reduced commercial shipping.US President Donald Trump last week said that “all mines” in the strait’s international waters had been removed or detonated, a claim subsequently confirmed by the US military. However, maritime security experts and shipowners remain cautious about declaring the entire waterway safe.The International Maritime Organization said in June that around 80 mines had been placed in vital shipping lanes. Iran has claimed it laid mines in international and Omani waters, while Tehran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in late August that “no one except Iran knows the location of these mines”.How the US is hunting mines underwaterTraditional minesweeping is already a painstaking process in peacetime. Specialised vessels typically move repeatedly across designated areas, locating mines, cutting them from their moorings and destroying them once they surface.The US operation in Hormuz has relied instead on a smaller and more discreet force.According to the Financial Times, US Navy divers used inflatable-hulled craft while robot boats and submersibles helped locate suspected Iranian mines. These systems can tow sonar arrays equipped with high-resolution, side-looking sensors capable of identifying objects on the seabed.The technology allows large areas to be searched while keeping personnel away from potentially explosive devices.But detection is only the beginning. “That is usually followed up by a navy diver who’s got to get in the water and approach the mine, and then put a charge on it and destroy it,” Bill Hamblet, a retired US Navy captain who often operated in the Gulf told FT.Hamblet described the operation as a “very small, lightweight kind of force” and said the US may have staged some operations from the USS Miguel Keith, an expeditionary mobile base attached to Gulf naval forces.Robotic underwater systems can also destroy mines by carrying explosives directly to them. Bryan Clark, a demining expert at the Hudson Institute, said systems such as Britain's SeaFox or the US AN/ASQ-235 Archerfish could be used for the task.Why Hormuz is so difficult to clearThe danger does not end once mines are located. “Mine-clearing forces are vulnerable because the operation is slow and their boats or helicopters lack defences,” said Clark.No US casualties have been reported specifically in connection with the demining operation. The challenge is also complicated by the physical geography and traffic patterns of the Strait. According to Chatham House, suspected minefields are believed to be located around the western entrance, the central eastbound shipping lane, the central westbound lane and the eastern exit towards the Gulf of Oman.Iran is believed to have thousands of Maham mines, including Maham 3 and Maham 7 variants. Some are designed to detonate when struck by ships, while others can respond to changes in electromagnetic fields as vessels pass overhead.The mines are particularly difficult to detect because they can interfere with the sonar systems used by minesweepers, according to Chatham House.Before the war, Iran was estimated to possess about 5,000 to 6,000 sea mines, many produced domestically. Analysts also believe Tehran retains a large proportion of its small boats and minelaying vessels.Two routes, but neither is idealWith the main central shipping route effectively closed, vessels have been using two alternative passages.Iran has established a northern route closer to its coastline, while the US has directed ships towards a southern route hugging Oman's coast, which Washington says ships can “freely and safely transit.”Both routes create problems. The alternative passages push ships towards the shallow edges of the Strait, increasing the risk of grounding. Their narrowness also limits traffic.Chatham House said only about 25 ships were transiting the Strait daily at the time of its assessment, compared with a pre-war average of roughly 125. Around 500 to 600 ships were still stranded in the Persian Gulf.Shipping cannot return to normal levels without reopening the main central channel. The problem is further complicated by ships switching off their automatic identification systems, or AIS, to avoid detection by Iranian forces. While this can reduce the risk of attack, it also makes it harder for vessels to know where other ships are, raising the possibility of collisions.GPS jamming across the Gulf has added another layer of difficulty by disrupting navigation and AIS signals.The bigger threat may be re-miningEven if the current mines are successfully cleared, the US faces the possibility that Iran could lay new ones.“It’s hard to know what to believe,” said Ethan Connell, assistant director of Taiwan Security Monitor and an expert on mines. “Iran is certainly trying to re-mine.“It’s always possible the [US] navy missed some. But the bigger and more pertinent issue, certainly the most annoying and expensive one, is the threat of re-mining.”On August 30, the US military struck Iranian rocket launchers that it said were preparing to fire sea mines into the Strait.Hamblet said rocket-fired mines could be significantly smaller than conventional mines deployed by ships and boats, potentially weighing about 50kg compared with mines weighing 500kg or 1,000kg.Iranian media has also claimed that at least two tankers struck mines in the past week, while an Iranian military spokesperson said Tehran had laid additional mines close to Oman.However, no mine attacks have been independently confirmed by maritime authorities during the conflict. Analysts said satellite imagery had also failed to provide clear evidence supporting Iran's claims.The only confirmed mine sighting in the Strait was reported by a Pakistani hydrographer in May.“It doesn’t take much to put a mine back in because there is a lot of small-boat traffic going across Hormuz every night”, a tanker industry executive said.Mines have become an information weaponThe uncertainty itself has become a strategic weapon. Even without confirmed mines, the possibility that they remain in the water is enough to deter shipowners and drive up insurance costs. According to the Financial Times, insurance for some vessels has risen to as much as 10 times pre-war levels, potentially adding around $10mn to the cost of insuring a typical supertanker.Oil prices initially fell about 5 per cent after Trump's declaration that the mines had been cleared, although they subsequently recovered their losses as strikes resumed.Hamblet said: “The Iranians have realised that their strongest card is the perception that they control the Strait of Hormuz. If they can convince the world that they can threaten the strait, that’s their strongest source of strategic leverage.”For Washington, the challenge is therefore not necessarily proving that every mine has been removed. It is convincing commercial operators that the route is safe enough to use.That is difficult when missile and drone attacks remain another threat to shipping.Hamblet said: “The bigger game is on the information side. That may be as important, if not more important, than what’s actually happening in the water or on the bottom of the strait.”Why international help will be neededThe US has sophisticated drones, robotic systems and helicopters for detecting and destroying mines, but it cannot realistically clear the Strait alone.Chatham House said the US currently had only one mine-clearing ship available in the Middle East and has historically relied on NATO allies for specialist mine-countermeasure capabilities.Britain, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Italy and other European partners have been identified as potential contributors to a multinational effort. Britain has also offered newer unmanned mine-warfare capabilities, while other European naval forces possess specialised mine-countermeasure equipment.Iran could also have an important role because it is believed to possess information about the location, types and settings of the mines it laid.However, Tehran's involvement would require political guarantees and international coordination.Demining is ultimately a political problemThe technical challenge of finding and destroying mines may be formidable, but the larger obstacle is ensuring that mine-clearance teams can operate without becoming targets.Mine-clearing vessels need predictable operating conditions and protection from renewed hostilities. Any lasting reopening of the Strait would therefore require the US, Iran and regional and international maritime partners to maintain a sustained cessation of attacks.Chatham House has argued that mine clearance could itself become part of a wider diplomatic process. Iranian participation could demonstrate a commitment to de-escalation, while international involvement could provide transparency and reassurance to other countries.The central issue is not simply how quickly mines can be removed. It is whether the political conditions can prevent them from being laid again.Technology can locate and destroy the explosives, but keeping the Strait open will ultimately depend on whether Iran, the US and other stakeholders can establish enough trust to prevent Hormuz from becoming a battlefield again.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
